A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FeatInv work. Their main text, tables, figures, algorithm, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including material relocated between the appendices and main text.

before.justification: v1 reports original ImageNet reconstruction experiments, cross-model evaluations, encoder and guidance ablations, BAID reconstructions, and feature-manipulation demonstrations.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds RCDM comparisons, intermediate-layer experiments, ImageNet-A and ImageNet-C evaluations, and reconstruction-variability analyses.

M1.justification: The frozen MiniSD backbone, ControlNet conditioning, convolutional feature encoder, noise-prediction objective, and FeatInv-Viz procedure remain unchanged. The intermediate-layer experiments reuse the existing procedure with layer-specific dimensions; control and guidance tuning changes concern experimental settings.

E1.justification: v2 adds ImageNet-A natural adversarial images and ImageNet-C corruption scenarios, substantially extending evaluation beyond ordinary ImageNet images and the already-used BAID dataset. ImageNet training and BAID coverage are retained; the additional concept examples remain within existing ImageNet coverage.

E2.justification: v1 discusses Bordes et al.'s approach without evaluating it directly. v2 Appendix A.5 and Table 4 introduce RCDM as an evaluated competing inversion method, using supplied ResNet50 weights and an independently trained ConvNeXt variant. This materially expands comparison beyond FeatInv variants and the MiniSD baseline.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes tuning from FID-based selection of fixed guidance scales to model-specific control-strength and guidance selection using classification agreement. Tables 1 and 3 change spatial cosine-similarity aggregation from median to mean. Added protocols include one-epoch intermediate-layer training, control/guidance sweeps using one image per class, and native-resolution versus resized RCDM evaluation.

E4.justification: Appendix A.2 replaces the ConvNeXt guidance-only FID/cosine-distance analysis with joint control-strength/guidance analyses across three backbones. v2 also adds intermediate-layer analyses, different-seed reconstruction examples, ImageNet-A/C robustness tests, and four additional concept-steering case studies. The earlier BAID and spatial-composition analyses are retained, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly states that the main evaluation generates one sample per feature map and adds qualitative variation across different random seeds in Appendix A.3. The five matched-seed reconstruction pairs used by FeatInv-Viz remain unchanged. Neither version reports confidence intervals, significance tests, or quantitative uncertainty estimates for the benchmark results.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 revise many results: unpooled ResNet50 top5/top1 agreement changes from 87%/63% to 91%/70%, while unpooled ConvNeXt FID changes from 7.14 to 8.20. These are revised results under changed settings, not established same-setting gains. v2 also adds RCDM, intermediate-layer, and corruption results, plus aggregate BAID results and ImageNet-A agreement of 71%/38%.

T1.justification: The concept-subspace decomposition and mathematical operations in Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. No new theorems, proofs, or formal assumptions appear. The added description of faithfulness is informal, while the cosine-aggregation revision concerns evaluation.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the central claims about probabilistic spatial feature inversion and its two applications. The introduction expands the explicit contribution list to claim demonstrated generalizability across ConvNeXt stages and robustness to corrupted inputs.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation of applicability and failure conditions: it discusses intermediate representations' reduced sensitivity to pixel deviations and failures to reproduce severe noise and contrast corruption. Appendix A.5 adds arguments about pretrained diffusion efficiency while acknowledging resolution differences and possible incomplete RCDM convergence. The original limitations paragraph is retained.

D1.justification: v2 adds RCDM weight/code provenance and training resources, intermediate feature-map dimensions, and suggested uniform control settings. The main FeatInv training recipe and code link remain. Reproducibility still has ambiguities: selected model-specific settings are not explicitly tabulated, and Appendix A.5 describes a FeatInv batch size of two while Section 2 states eight.

R1.justification: v2 adds Preechakul et al.'s diffusion autoencoders and distinguishes their global latent codes from spatial feature conditioning. It also adds the ImageNet-A/C references and expands the discussion of the already-cited RCDM approach. The central novelty positioning remains unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose, including the abstract, methods, conclusion, and limitations, remains closely matched. v2 clarifies faithfulness terminology, creates a dedicated robustness subsection, reorganizes appendices, and moves BAID and spatial-composition discussion into the main text. These are localized revisions rather than a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the guidance line plot with control/guidance heatmaps and adds intermediate-layer charts, seed-variation grids, corruption plots and image panels, an RCDM comparison table, and further concept visualizations. Existing BAID and spatial-composition figures move into the main text. The document also adopts a different publication layout.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation by adding a direct competing-method comparison and systematic tests of intermediate layers, adversarial images, and corruption severity. These address v1's limited evidence about comparative effectiveness and where faithful reconstruction fails. Unequal RCDM resolutions, possible incomplete convergence, and reporting inconsistencies—including calling lower RCDM FID values higher—temper the conclusions, but the added validation and concrete failure boundaries provide a substantial overall improvement.
